title: General Nature of Partnership
outcomes: Explain the Section 4 definitions of partnership, partner, firm and firm name, and the five elements that must all be present.
Apply the true test of partnership (Sections 5 and 6) to decide whether a given relationship is a partnership.
Distinguish a partnership from a company, an HUF business, co-ownership, a club and an association.
Classify partnerships (at will, fixed period, particular, general) and partners (active, sleeping, nominal, profits-only, sub-partner, incoming, outgoing, by holding out).

meta.exam_tip: Expect a 4-mark problem on "is this a partnership?" or "holding out", and a distinction question. Always state the true test (Section 6 / mutual agency) before applying it.

concepts.title: Definitions in Section 4: partnership, partner, firm, firm name
body: Section 4 describes partnership as a relationship: it exists between people who have agreed to divide among themselves the profits of a business that is run by all of them, or by one or more of them on behalf of all.
Each person in that relationship is a "partner". Taken together, the partners are the "firm". The name under which they trade is the "firm name".
A firm is therefore only a convenient collective label. In law it has no personality of its own apart from the partners — unlike a company.
concepts.analogy: A "firm" is like the word "team": it is a handy name for a group of players, but the team cannot sign a contract apart from its players.
concepts.work: When a CA writes "M/s Shah & Mehta" in an audit report or tax return, the legal reality is the group of partners. That is why partners sign the return and why personal assets are at risk for firm debts.

concepts.title: Five elements of partnership
body: 1. Association of two or more persons. Only persons recognised by law can contract, so a firm as such cannot be a partner in another firm; a minor cannot be a partner but may be admitted to the benefits with the consent of all partners. The Partnership Act sets no upper limit, but Section 464 of the Companies Act, 2013 caps it at 100 and the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 currently fix the limit at 50.

2. Agreement. Partnership is voluntary and contractual. The agreement may be written or oral, express or implied from conduct; Section 5 adds that the relationship arises from contract, not from status.

3. Business. Section 2(b) treats every trade, occupation and profession as business. There must be a business, and the aim must be to earn gains — a charitable or social body cannot be run as a partnership.

4. Agreement to share profits. A person who takes the entire profit cannot be a partner with the others. Sharing losses is not an essential element — some partners may agree to bear all losses — but unless agreed otherwise, losses follow the profit-sharing ratio.

5. Mutual agency — the business is run by all the partners or by any of them on behalf of all. Each working partner is both principal (bound by others' acts) and agent (binds the others). In CIT v. K.D. Kamath & Co. the Supreme Court held that giving one partner exclusive control of management or the bank account does not by itself negate partnership, so long as the profit-sharing agreement and the mutual agency exist.
concepts.analogy: Think of a five-legged table: number, agreement, business, profit-sharing and mutual agency. Remove any leg and it is not a partnership table any more.
concepts.work: Bankers and tax officers often ask a CA to certify that a "partnership" is genuine. The CA checks the deed, the bank account in the firm name, the profit-sharing clause and who actually runs the business — the five elements in practice.

concepts.title: True test of partnership (Sections 5 and 6)
body: Section 6: to decide whether a group is a firm or whether someone is a partner, look at the real relation between the parties shown by all the relevant facts taken together — not merely the label they use.
Agreement, not status (Section 5): members of a Hindu Undivided Family running the family business are not partners in it, because their relationship comes from birth, not contract.

Profit sharing is only prima facie evidence. Co-owners who share the gross returns of jointly held property are not partners for that reason alone. Nor do the following become partners merely because they receive a share of profits or a profit-linked payment: a lender to the business, an employee or agent paid by way of remuneration, the widow or child of a deceased partner receiving an annuity, and a former owner receiving part of the profits as the price of goodwill.

Mutual agency is the decisive test (Cox v. Hickman is the classic English authority). In Santiranjan Das Gupta v. Dasyran Murzamull the Supreme Court found no partnership because, among other things, no record of terms was kept, the "firm" had no accounts or bank account of its own, and the authorities were never told of it.
concepts.analogy: Calling a cat a dog does not make it bark. Courts listen for the bark — real agency and real profit-sharing — not the label on the collar.
concepts.work: Profit-linked bonuses to employees, revenue-share loans and goodwill payouts are common. A CA must make sure the documents do not accidentally create a partnership (and unlimited liability) where none was intended.

concepts.title: Partnership distinguished from other forms of organisation
body: The comparison tables below cover company, HUF, co-ownership, club and association. In an exam, choose 4–6 bases and write each one as a pair of short contrasting lines.

Remember the anchors: a company is a separate person with limited liability and perpetual succession; an HUF arises by birth and only the Karta has unlimited liability; co-ownership need not involve business or agency; a club or association has no profit motive.

blocks.title: Partnership compared with other forms

concepts.analogy: A partnership is a group of people who are also each other's agents; a company is a new "person" the group creates; an HUF is a family that happens to own a business.
concepts.work: Choosing between a firm, an LLP and a private company is a regular advisory task. Liability, number of members, compliance cost and transferability — the same bases as in these tables — drive the advice.

concepts.title: Kinds of partnership and the partnership deed
body: By duration: a partnership at will (Section 7) has no fixed term and no clause on how it will end — any partner may dissolve it by written notice to all the others. A partnership for a fixed period ends when the term expires; if the partners simply carry on, it becomes a partnership at will.
By extent of business: a particular partnership (Section 8) is formed for a single venture or undertaking and ends on its completion; a general partnership is formed to carry on business generally.

Partnership deed: no particular form is required, but a written, stamped deed avoids disputes. Where immovable property is brought in, the instrument must be in writing, stamped and registered. Typical clauses: firm name, partners, nature and place of business, date of start and duration, capital, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital/drawings/loans, salaries or commission, admission and retirement, expulsion, and settlement of accounts on dissolution.

Basis

On expiry of the term — if business continues, it becomes a partnership at will

blocks.title: Kinds of partnership

concepts.analogy: A partnership at will is a rented flat with no lock-in — either side can leave on notice. A fixed-period partnership is a lease with a set end date.
concepts.work: Drafting or reviewing the deed is core CA work: income-tax rules allow interest and remuneration to partners only if the deed authorises them, so a missing clause can cost the firm a deduction.

concepts.title: Types of partners
body: Active (actual / ostensible) partner: a partner by agreement who takes part in running the business; he must give public notice on retirement to avoid liability for later acts.
Sleeping or dormant partner: shares profits and losses and is liable to outsiders, but takes no active part; public notice of his retirement is not required.
Nominal partner: lends only his name, has no real interest and no share of profits, yet is liable to third parties for the firm's acts.

Partner in profits only: shares profits but is exempt from losses as between partners; still liable to outsiders. Sub-partner: someone who shares one partner's profit share by private arrangement — he is not a partner of the firm, has no rights against it and no liability for its debts.

Incoming partner: admitted with the consent of all existing partners; not liable for acts before his admission. Outgoing partner: leaves while the others continue; liable to third parties for the firm's acts until public notice of his retirement is given.

Partner by holding out (Section 28) — partnership by estoppel: a person who by words or conduct represents himself as a partner, or knowingly allows himself to be so represented, is liable as a partner to anyone who gave credit to the firm on the faith of that representation. Fraudulent intent need not be shown, and only the person who relied on the representation can enforce this liability. It also catches a retired partner whose name continues to be used without public notice.

blocks.title: Types of partners at a glance

concepts.analogy: Holding out is like letting someone introduce you as the co-signer of a loan. If the lender relies on it, you cannot later say "I never signed".
concepts.work: Before lending, banks ask who the partners are. If a retired partner's name is still on letterheads, he may remain exposed. CAs advise clients to give public notice and update letterheads, GST and bank records at once.

illustrations.title: Lender paid out of profits — partner or not?
illustrations.q: Rekha lends ₹6,00,000 to Vardhan Traders, a firm of two partners. Instead of fixed interest, the loan agreement gives her 15% of the firm's yearly profit until the loan is repaid. She has no say in the business. The firm defaults on a supplier's bill and the supplier sues Rekha as a partner. Advise.

solution.provision: Section 6: whether a person is a partner is decided by the real relation between the parties, judged from all relevant facts. Receiving a share of profits, or a payment that varies with profits, does not of itself make a person a partner; in particular a lender who is paid out of profits is not a partner for that reason alone. Mutual agency is the true test (Section 4).
solution.facts: Rekha advanced money as a loan and is repaid through a profit-linked return. She takes no part in the business and nobody acts on her behalf.
solution.analysis: The only link is the profit-linked return on her loan, which Section 6 expressly says is not conclusive. There is no agreement that the business is run by the partners on her behalf, so the element of mutual agency is missing.
solution.conclusion: Rekha is a creditor of the firm, not a partner. The supplier cannot hold her liable for the firm's debt.

illustrations.title: An employee introduced as a partner
illustrations.q: Arun and Bhushan run Arun Bhushan & Co. At a trade fair Arun introduces Chetan, the firm's sales manager, to a wholesaler, Dhillon, saying "Chetan is our third partner." Chetan smiles and says nothing. Relying on this, Dhillon supplies goods worth ₹3,40,000 on credit. The firm does not pay. Can Dhillon recover from Chetan?

solution.provision: Section 28 (holding out): a person who, by what he says or writes or by how he behaves, presents himself as a partner — or knowingly lets others present him so — must answer as a partner to anyone who extended credit to the firm because of that representation. It does not matter whether the person making the representation knew it had reached the creditor, and fraud need not be proved.
solution.facts: Arun represented Chetan as a partner in Chetan's presence. Chetan stayed silent. Dhillon gave credit relying on that statement.
solution.analysis: By staying silent when he heard himself described as a partner, Chetan knowingly permitted the representation. Dhillon acted on it by supplying goods on credit. All the conditions of Section 28 are met even though Chetan is only an employee.
solution.conclusion: Chetan is liable as a partner by holding out. Dhillon can recover ₹3,40,000 from Arun, Bhushan and Chetan.

illustrations.title: Family business and partnership
illustrations.q: Three brothers, members of a Hindu Undivided Family, carry on the ancestral cloth business run by the eldest brother as Karta. No agreement has ever been made among them. A creditor argues that all three are partners with unlimited liability. Is the creditor right?

solution.provision: Section 5: partnership is created by contract, never by status. So members of a Hindu Undivided Family who run the family business in that capacity do not thereby become partners.
solution.facts: The brothers are coparceners by birth. The business is ancestral and they never entered into a partnership agreement.
solution.analysis: Their rights arise from status under Hindu law. Without a contract there is no partnership. In an HUF business only the Karta has unlimited liability; the other coparceners are liable only to the extent of their interest in the family property.
solution.conclusion: The creditor is wrong. The brothers are not partners; only the Karta is personally liable without limit.

illustrations.title: Fixed-term firm that carries on
illustrations.q: Isha and Jatin formed a partnership for three years ending 31 March 2026 to run a coaching centre. They kept running it after that date without any fresh agreement. In August 2026 Isha wants to end the partnership immediately. Jatin says she must wait for a new three-year term. Advise Isha.

solution.provision: Section 7: where no period is fixed and no provision is made for the end of the partnership, it is a partnership at will. Section 17(b) adds that when a firm formed for a fixed term carries on after the term, the partners' rights stay the same so far as they fit a partnership at will. Under Section 43, any one partner can end a partnership at will by sending written notice of dissolution to every other partner.
solution.facts: The fixed term ended on 31 March 2026. The partners carried on without fixing a new term.
solution.analysis: From 1 April 2026 the firm is a partnership at will. There is no new three-year term. Isha may dissolve it by written notice to Jatin; the firm is dissolved from the date stated in the notice or, if none, from the date the notice is communicated.
solution.conclusion: Isha can end the partnership by written notice; Jatin's claim of a new fixed term is wrong.

jobs.title: Is our profit-share employee a partner?
jobs.role: CA in practice advising a family firm
jobs.situation: A firm wants to retain its star sales head by paying him 5% of net profit instead of a fixed bonus. The partners worry this will make him a partner with rights over the business.
steps: Explain Section 6: a profit-linked payment to an employee as remuneration does not by itself make him a partner.
Draft the letter as an employment contract: salary plus profit-linked incentive, no authority to bind the firm, no capital, no share in losses.
Make sure he is never described as a "partner" on cards, emails or letterheads — Section 28 (holding out) could otherwise create liability.
Record the incentive as an employee cost in the books, not as a profit appropriation.
jobs.takeaway: Profit sharing alone is not partnership; mutual agency is. Good drafting and consistent conduct keep the relationship clear.
jobs.think: What single fact would most strongly suggest that he had become a partner?
jobs.answer: If the business were carried on on his behalf too — for example, if he could bind the firm and the others acted as his agents — that mutual agency would point to partnership.

jobs.title: Choosing the form for a start-up of three friends
jobs.situation: Three friends want to open a café chain. One will invest but not work; two will run it. They ask whether a partnership firm is suitable.
steps: Explain the features: easy to form, no compulsory registration, but unlimited liability and no separate legal personality.
Note that the investor would be a sleeping partner — still fully liable to outsiders.
Compare with a private company or an LLP if they want limited liability or plan to bring in investors.
If they choose a firm, draft a deed covering capital, ratio, interest, salaries for working partners and exit terms.
jobs.takeaway: The comparison bases in this unit are exactly what a client needs to choose a business form.
jobs.think: Why might the non-working investor prefer a company?
jobs.answer: As a sleeping partner he would have unlimited liability for the firm's debts; as a shareholder his liability would be limited to the unpaid amount on his shares.

jobs.title: Retired partner still on the letterhead
jobs.role: Articled assistant during a statutory audit of a firm's major customer
jobs.situation: You notice that a partner who retired a year ago still appears on the firm's letterhead and bank mandate.
steps: Flag the risk: under Sections 28 and 32 a retired partner can be held liable to creditors who deal with the firm believing he is still a partner, until public notice is given.
Suggest the firm give public notice of retirement and inform its bank, suppliers and the Registrar of Firms.
Ask for revised letterheads and bank mandates.
jobs.takeaway: Holding out can arise from carelessness, not just from false statements.

mcqs.q: The terms "partnership", "partner", "firm" and "firm name" are defined in which section of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932?
The true (decisive) test of a partnership is:
mcqs.explain: Profit sharing is only prima facie evidence (Section 6); mutual agency — the business being run by all or any one of them on behalf of all — is the real test.

mcqs.q: Under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 read with Section 464 of the Companies Act, 2013, the maximum number of partners in a firm is:
mcqs.explain: Section 464 permits a ceiling of up to 100; the Rules currently fix it at 50.

mcqs.q: Which of the following persons becomes a partner merely because he receives a share of the profits?
options: None of these, by that fact alone
A lender paid out of profits
An employee paid a profit-linked bonus
The widow of a deceased partner receiving an annuity out of profits
mcqs.explain: Section 6 says each of these receipts does not of itself make the receiver a partner.

mcqs.q: A partnership in which no period is fixed and no provision is made for its determination is:
options: A partnership for a fixed period

mcqs.q: Members of an HUF carrying on the family business as such are:
options: Not partners, because partnership arises from contract, not status
Partners only if the Karta agrees

mcqs.q: A person who lends only his name to the firm, has no real interest and does not share profits, is a:
mcqs.explain: He is still liable to third parties for the firm's acts.

mcqs.q: Which partner need NOT give public notice of retirement to escape liability for later acts of the firm?
mcqs.explain: Outsiders did not know him as a partner, so no public notice is required.

mcqs.q: A partner agrees to share his profit share with an outsider, who thereby becomes a:
options: Sub-partner — no rights against the firm and no liability for its debts
mcqs.explain: The arrangement is private between the partner and the outsider.

mcqs.q: Two persons jointly own a building and share the rent received. They are:
mcqs.explain: Sharing gross returns from jointly held property does not of itself create partnership; there is no business carried on for each other.

mcqs.q: Liability arising from "holding out" (Section 28) can be enforced by:
options: Only the person who gave credit relying on the representation
mcqs.explain: The liability rests on estoppel in favour of the person who acted on the representation.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a feature of a partnership firm?
mcqs.explain: Perpetual succession belongs to a company; a firm is ordinarily dissolved by the death of a partner unless agreed otherwise.

mcqs.q: A firm formed to construct a single building and to end on its completion is a:
mcqs.explain: Section 8 — a partnership for a particular adventure or undertaking.

questions.q: Kiran and Lalit are partners in K L Enterprises. Lalit introduces Manav, a family friend, to a supplier, Nirmal, as "our new partner". Manav, who is present, does not object. Nirmal supplies 40 air-conditioners on credit to the firm, relying on Manav's presence. The firm fails to pay and Nirmal sues Kiran, Lalit and Manav. Manav pleads that he never signed any partnership deed. Decide with reference to the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

model.provision: Section 28: whoever, by words or conduct, holds himself out as a partner, or knowingly lets himself be held out as one, is answerable as a partner to every person who gave the firm credit because of that representation. Fraudulent intention need not be shown.
model.facts: Manav was described as a partner in his presence and did not object. Nirmal supplied goods on credit relying on that representation.
model.analysis: Manav's silence amounts to knowingly permitting the representation. The absence of a partnership deed is irrelevant because liability under Section 28 rests on estoppel, not on agreement. Nirmal is the very person who acted on the representation.
model.conclusion: Manav is liable as a partner by holding out. Nirmal can recover the price from Kiran, Lalit and Manav.

scheme.pt: Silence = knowingly permitting; credit given on faith of representation
Deed / agreement not needed for this liability
Conclusion: Manav liable; Nirmal can recover

remarks: Most candidates identify holding out; full marks go to those who explain that silence is "knowingly permitting" and that Nirmal relied on it.
Writing only "Manav is liable" without the provision earns at most one mark.
mistakes: Saying Manav is not liable because there was no agreement.
Treating Manav as a sleeping partner.
Forgetting to mention that the creditor relied on the representation.
tips: Use the four headings: Provision, Facts, Analysis, Conclusion.
Quote "Section 28" and the phrase "partner by holding out (estoppel)".

questions.q: State, giving reasons, whether a partnership exists in each case: (a) Two co-owners of an inherited flat share the rent equally. (b) Pallavi and Qadir buy 500 bags of onions jointly, agreeing to sell them and share the profit equally. (c) The manager of a shop is paid 10% of its net profit in addition to his salary. (d) Rohit, a lender, receives a share of the firm's profits as interest on his loan.

model.text: Section 4 requires an agreement to share the profits of a business that is run by all the persons concerned or by any of them on behalf of all. Section 6 says the real relation, seen from all the facts, decides; a share of profits alone is not conclusive.

items: (a) No partnership — co-owners sharing the gross return of jointly held property are not partners merely for that reason (Section 6); there is no business and no mutual agency.
(b) Partnership (a particular partnership under Section 8) — they agreed to carry on a business venture jointly and share its profit; each acts for both.
(c) No partnership — a servant or agent receiving a share of profits as remuneration does not thereby become a partner (Section 6).
(d) No partnership — a lender receiving a share of profits is not a partner by that fact alone (Section 6); he does not carry on the business and nobody acts for him.

scheme.pt: States Section 4 elements and Section 6 test

remarks: Each part carries one mark only if the reason is given; a bare "yes/no" earns nothing.
Candidates who state the true test first answer all four parts more quickly and consistently.
mistakes: Treating any profit sharing as conclusive proof of partnership.
Missing that (b) is a partnership because of the joint venture.
tips: State the rule once at the top, then answer each part in two lines.
Name the category in Section 6 (co-owner, servant, lender) for each "no".

questions.q: Distinguish between a partnership and a Hindu Undivided Family business on any four bases.

head: Basis
Partnership
HUF business
rows: By birth — status under Hindu law
Death of a partner ordinarily dissolves the firm
Death of a member does not affect the family business
Every partner may take part and can bind the firm
Management vests in the Karta, who alone binds the family business
Karta unlimited; other coparceners only to the extent of their interest
Can only be admitted to benefits, with all partners' consent

remarks: A table with four clear bases is the fastest way to full marks.
mistakes: Writing about partnership only, without the HUF contrast on the same basis.
Saying all coparceners have unlimited liability.
tips: Keep each cell to one line.
Put the most important bases first: creation, liability, death.

questions.q: Explain the essential elements of a partnership under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

model.text: Under Section 4, partnership is the relationship of people who agree to divide the profits of a business that all of them, or any one of them on behalf of all, carry on. The elements are:

items: Association of two or more persons — persons competent to contract; a minor only for benefits; at most 50 partners (Companies Act, 2013, Section 464 read with the 2014 Rules).
Agreement — oral or written, express or implied; partnership arises from contract, not status (Section 5).
Business — includes every trade, occupation and profession (Section 2(b)); the aim must be gain.
Agreement to share profits — losses ordinarily follow the profit ratio but agreement to share losses is not essential.
Mutual agency — the business is run by all or any of them on behalf of all; each partner is both principal and agent. This is the true test (Section 6).

model.text: All five must exist together for a partnership to come into existence.

scheme.pt: Two or more persons, with limit
Mutual agency as the true test

remarks: Answers that explain mutual agency as the cardinal element score higher.
mistakes: Listing "registration" or "written deed" as an essential element.
Saying losses must always be shared.
tips: Number the elements; one line of explanation each.

summary: Section 4: partnership = relation of persons who agree to share profits of a business run by all or any of them for all. Partners individually; firm collectively; firm name = trading name.
Five elements: 2+ persons (max 50), agreement, business, profit sharing, mutual agency.
Section 5: contract, not status (HUF members are not partners). Section 6: real relation from all facts; profit sharing only prima facie; mutual agency is the true test.
Kinds: at will (Section 7), fixed period, particular (Section 8), general.
Partners: active, sleeping, nominal, profits-only, sub-partner, incoming, outgoing, by holding out (Section 28).
remember: Lender, employee, widow/child annuitant, seller of goodwill — sharing profits does not by itself make them partners.
Fixed-term firm continued after expiry → partnership at will.
Holding out: liability only to the person who gave credit relying on the representation; no fraud needed.
traps: Don't call registration or a written deed an essential element.
Don't treat sharing of losses as essential.
Don't say a sub-partner is liable to the firm's creditors.
Don't confuse a sleeping partner (shares profits) with a nominal partner (lends only his name).

quickref.v: Definitions: partnership, partner, firm, firm name
Partnership arises from contract, not status
Real relation from all facts; profit sharing not conclusive
Up to 100 partners allowed by Act; Rules fix 50

viva.q: Define partnership under Section 4 and name its essential elements.
viva.model: Partnership is the relationship of people who agree to divide the profits of a business that all of them run, or that any one of them runs on behalf of all. The essentials are an association of two or more persons, an agreement between them, a business, an agreement to share profits, and mutual agency, meaning one partner can run the business on behalf of all.

viva.q: Distinguish between a sleeping partner and a nominal partner.
viva.model: A sleeping or dormant partner invests and shares profits and losses but does not take an active part in the business, and he need not give public notice of retirement. A nominal partner only lends his name, does not invest, does not share profits and takes no part in the business. Both are liable to third parties for the acts of the firm.

viva.q: What is a partnership at will, and how can it be dissolved?
viva.model: Under Section 7 a partnership at will is one where no fixed period is agreed and there is no provision for how the partnership will come to an end. Any partner can dissolve it by sending a written notice to all the other partners. A fixed-term firm that carries on after its term also becomes a partnership at will.

cases.title: Sunrise Foods: who is really a partner?
cases.case: Sunrise Foods is run by Ajay and Bela, who share profits equally under an oral agreement. Their uncle Chandan lent ₹10,00,000 to the business and receives 10% of the yearly profit instead of interest. Deepa, Ajay's college friend, allowed Ajay to print her name as a "partner" on the firm's brochure to impress customers; she has no capital and takes no profit. Eshan, a supplier, saw the brochure and gave the firm credit of ₹4,00,000. Bela's cousin Farhan has a private arrangement with Bela to receive one-fourth of her share of profits. The firm has defaulted on Eshan's dues.

mcqs.q: Is the oral agreement between Ajay and Bela enough to form a partnership?
options: Yes — a partnership agreement may be oral or written
No — a written deed is compulsory
No — the firm must first be registered
Yes, but only for one year
mcqs.explain: Partnership arises from agreement, which may be oral, written or implied from conduct. Registration and a written deed are not essential to its existence.

options: A creditor — a lender paid out of profits is not a partner for that reason alone
A partner, because he shares profits
mcqs.explain: Section 6 expressly says receipt of a profit share by a lender does not of itself make him a partner; there is no mutual agency.

mcqs.q: Can Eshan hold Deepa liable for his ₹4,00,000?
options: Yes — she knowingly allowed herself to be represented as a partner and Eshan gave credit relying on it
No — she takes no share of profit
Only if she signed the brochure herself
mcqs.explain: Section 28 (holding out). Capital and profit share are irrelevant; reliance by the creditor is what matters.

options: A sub-partner — no rights against the firm and no liability for its debts
mcqs.explain: An arrangement to share one partner's profit share creates only a sub-partnership with that partner.
